client: I've been really struggling since my grandma passed away last month. I feel this heavy sadness all the time, and what makes it worse is seeing how devastated my mom is - I want to help her but I don't even know how to handle my own grief. Part of me wonders if talking about it will just make us both feel worse instead of better.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying both your own grief and concern for your mom, which must feel incredibly heavy right now. When you wonder if talking might make things worse, what thoughts come up about what could happen if you did share your feelings with her?

client: I worry that if I open up to my mom about how lonely and overwhelmed I feel, it'll just make her feel worse or guilty. She's already dealing with so much grief herself, and I don't want to burden her more. At the same time, keeping it all inside makes me feel even more isolated.
therapist: I hear how deeply you're trying to protect your mom while also feeling this painful isolation yourself. That tension between wanting connection and fearing you'll burden others is so understandable in grief. What do you imagine might happen if you shared just a small part of your feelings with her?

client: I don't know... every time I think about opening up to her, I freeze up. What if my sadness just makes her feel worse? She's already dealing with so much after dad died. I guess part of me worries she'll see me as weak or selfish for needing support too.
therapist: It sounds like there's a lot of fear holding you back from reaching out - both for her sake and how she might see you. That worry about being perceived as weak or selfish seems particularly painful to sit with. What evidence do you have about how your mom has responded to vulnerable moments between you two in the past?

client:
I guess when I was younger and would cry about school stress, my mom was usually pretty understanding. But that feels different from now - I'm an adult and she has her own health issues to deal with. I worry that opening up about my anxiety would just burden her when she's already struggling. 

Part of me knows she'd probably want to help, but another part keeps thinking "she has enough on her plate without my problems too." It's this constant back-and-forth in my head.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real tension between knowing your mom cares and fearing you'd be adding to her load - that back-and-forth must feel exhausting to carry. When you think back to times she's been supportive, what makes this current situation feel different to you?

client: I guess it feels different because she’s been so overwhelmed lately with her own health issues and work. It’s like I can see how much she’s struggling, and I don’t want to make it worse by adding my problems to her plate. Even though she’s been supportive in the past, I feel guilty for even thinking about leaning on her now. It’s like I’m stuck between needing her and not wanting to burden her.
therapist: That sense of being stuck between needing support and not wanting to add to her struggles sounds so hard to sit with. It's clear how much you care about her well being. What would it feel like to consider that sharing your feelings might actually help you both feel less alone in your grief, rather than being a burden?

client: I get what you're saying, but I just keep thinking about how fragile she seems right now. Whenever I start to open up, I see how exhausted she looks and immediately shut down. It feels selfish to add my pain on top of everything she's already dealing with.
therapist: I hear how deeply attuned you are to your mom's exhaustion, and how that makes you pull back from sharing your own pain. That protective instinct comes from such a caring place. What would it be like to explore other ways to process your grief that might feel less overwhelming than talking with your mom right now?

client:
I get what you're saying, but it's not just about finding other ways to process grief. The guilt comes from feeling like I *should* be able to talk to my mom about this stuff - she's my mom, you know? When I try journaling or talking to friends, it just makes me feel worse because it feels like I'm avoiding the real issue. 

And honestly? Sometimes I worry that if I don't keep checking on her, she'll completely fall apart. I know that's probably not rational, but the thought won't go away.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying this heavy sense of responsibility alongside your grief - both the "should" about talking to your mom and the fear about what might happen if you don't stay vigilant. That combination must feel incredibly draining. What do you think it would take to give yourself permission to let go of some of these expectations, even just a little?

client: I know logically that I should let go of some of these expectations, but the thought of doing that makes me feel even more guilty. Like if I stop worrying about my mom all the time, something bad will happen and it'll be my fault for not being careful enough. It's like my anxiety is the only thing keeping her safe.
therapist: That belief that your worry is somehow protecting your mom must feel both exhausting and strangely necessary right now. When you imagine letting go of some of that vigilance, what's the worst part of that thought for you?

client: The worst part is that if I stop worrying, something bad might actually happen to her. It feels like my anxiety is the only thing keeping her safe, even though I know that doesn’t make sense logically. But the idea of relaxing even a little makes me feel guilty, like I’m abandoning her somehow.
therapist: It's clear how deeply this fear and guilt have taken root, even though part of you recognizes they might not be entirely logical. That tug-of-war between knowing something intellectually but feeling it emotionally is so common in grief and anxiety. What would it feel like to experiment with setting aside just 10 minutes a day where you intentionally let go of that protective worry?

client: I get what you're saying about setting aside time, but the idea of intentionally letting go of worry makes me anxious. What if something bad happens during those 10 minutes because I wasn't being vigilant? And honestly, I'm not sure I even know how to "let go" - the guilt feels like part of me now.
therapist: It sounds like the very idea of releasing this worry brings up both fear and confusion - like trying to let go of something that's become part of how you function. That's completely understandable when you've been carrying this for so long. What would it feel like to start even smaller - maybe just noticing when the worry arises without needing to act on it right away?
